# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

import './style.css';
import './buy';
import { gsap } from 'gsap';
import { ScrollTrigger } from 'gsap/ScrollTrigger';

const reduce = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

if (!reduce) {
  gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);

  // Entrance: hidden states are set here, so a failed script leaves a complete page.
  gsap
    .timeline({ defaults: { ease: 'power3.out' } })
    .from('.bar', { y: -40, opacity: 0, duration: 0.6 })
    .from('.hero-copy > *', { y: 30, opacity: 0, duration: 0.7, stagger: 0.08 }, '-=0.3')
    .from('.demo', { y: 50, opacity: 0, duration: 0.9 }, '-=0.5')
    .from('.msg', { y: 14, opacity: 0, duration: 0.5, stagger: 0.25 }, '-=0.4');

  gsap.from('.stat', {
    scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.stats', start: 'top 85%' },
    y: 40, opacity: 0, duration: 0.8, stagger: 0.1, ease: 'back.out(1.6)',
  });
  gsap.from('.card', {
    scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.cards', start: 'top 85%' },
    y: 40, opacity: 0, duration: 0.7, stagger: 0.07, clearProps: 'opacity,transform',
  });

  // Count-up for the numeric stats, driven by data-num.
  document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('b[data-num]').forEach((el) => {
    const end = Number(el.dataset.num);
    const o = { v: 0 };
    gsap.to(o, {
      v: end, duration: 1.2, ease: 'power2.out',
      scrollTrigger: { trigger: el, start: 'top 90%' },
      onUpdate: () => { el.textContent = String(Math.round(o.v)); },
      onComplete: () => { el.textContent = String(end); },
    });
  });

  // Pointer tilt: GSAP owns the transform on these elements.
  const tilt = (el: HTMLElement, ry: number, rx: number, rest = { ry: 0, rx: 0 }) => {
    el.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
      const r = el.getBoundingClientRect();
      const x = (e.clientX - r.left) / r.width - 0.5;
      const y = (e.clientY - r.top) / r.height - 0.5;
      gsap.to(el, { rotationY: rest.ry + x * ry, rotationX: rest.rx - y * rx, transformPerspective: 1500, duration: 0.4 });
    });
    el.addEventListener('pointerleave', () => {
      gsap.to(el, { rotationY: rest.ry, rotationX: rest.rx, duration: 1, ease: 'elastic.out(1, .5)' });
    });
  };
  document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-tilt]').forEach((el) => tilt(el, 10, 8));
  const demo = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[data-tilt-demo]');
  if (demo) {
    gsap.set(demo, { rotationY: -8, rotationX: 4, transformPerspective: 1500 });
    tilt(demo, 10, 8, { ry: -8, rx: 4 });
  }
}

// Fire-and-forget analytics for the host's /api/analytics endpoints.
// No cookies; ids live in storage only so the host can count unique visitors.
function id(storage: Storage, key: string): string {
  try {
    let v = storage.getItem(key);
    if (!v) {
      v = crypto.randomUUID();
      storage.setItem(key, v);
    }
    return v;
  } catch {
    return '';
  }
}

const ids = () => ({
  visitor_id: id(localStorage, 'lk_vid'),
  session_id: id(sessionStorage, 'lk_sid'),
});

function post(url: string, body: unknown): void {
  try {
    void fetch(url, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
      keepalive: true,
    }).catch(() => {});
  } catch { /* analytics never breaks the page */ }
}

export function trackPageview(): void {
  const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
  post('/api/analytics/pageview', {
    path: location.pathname,
    referrer: document.referrer,
    screen: `${window.screen.width}x${window.screen.height}`,
    utm_source: q.get('utm_source') ?? undefined,
    utm_medium: q.get('utm_medium') ?? undefined,
    utm_campaign: q.get('utm_campaign') ?? undefined,
    utm_term: q.get('utm_term') ?? undefined,
    utm_content: q.get('utm_content') ?? undefined,
    ...ids(),
  });
}

// checkout_start is recorded by the server; never send it from here.
export function trackEvent(event: 'view_tool', tool: string): void {
  post('/api/analytics/event', { event, tool, path: location.pathname, ...ids() });
}

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).

  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Bundled Manuals

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

customer-facing elements.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/branding","type":"docs","content":"# Branding your Stripe account\nCustomize the appearance of your Stripe account and customer-facing elements.\nCustomize the appearance of your emails, checkout, payment links, customer portal, and invoices in your [Branding settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/account/branding).\n> #### Customize with an agent\n>\n> You can view and update your branding settings with the [Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli) or the [Stripe MCP server](https://docs.stripe.com/mcp). To find the available operations, run `stripe tools search branding` in the CLI, or ask your AI agent to search for `branding` using Stripe MCP.\n[Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IWpbEcdocUI)\n## Branding\nIcons and logos must be in JPG or PNG format, less than 512kb in size, and equal to or greater than 128px by 128px.\n- **Icon**—A square, digital-friendly icon or logo.\n- **Logo**—A non-square logo to override some uses of the icon.\n- **Brand color**—Used on receipts, invoices, and the customer portal.\n- **Accent color**—Used as a background on emails and pages.\n### Apply brand settings\nBrand settings apply to your whole account and take effect in many places.\n| Setting          | Emails                 | Checkout & Payment Links | Customer portal | Hosted invoice page | Invoice PDFs |\n| ---------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------- | ------------------- | ------------ |\n| **Icon**         | Yes                    | Yes                      | Yes             | Yes                 | Yes          |\n| **Logo**         | No                     | Yes                      | No              | No                  | Yes          |\n| **Brand color**  | Yes                    | No                       | Yes             | Yes                 | Yes          |\n| **Accent color** | Yes (background color) | Yes                      | Yes             | Yes                 | No           |\n### Branding with Connect\nConnect platforms can configure a connected account’s branding using [configuration.merchant.branding](https://docs.stripe.com/api/v2/core/accounts/object#v2_account_object-configuration-merchant-branding) (with the Accounts v2 API) or [settings.branding](https://docs.stripe.com/api/accounts/object#account_object-settings-branding) (with the Accounts v1 API). The branding of a given user interface depends on the integration:\n- For integrations that use *direct charges* (A charge type where customers transact directly with a connected account, which is always the merchant of record. With each payment, the connected account pays fees to Stripe and, optionally, to your platform), where objects usually exist on connected accounts, most interfaces use the connected account’s branding. Connect-related emails sent to a connected account, such as risk or onboarding communications, are an exception. Those emails use the platform’s branding.\n- For integrations that use *indirect charges* (A charge type where customers transact directly with your platform instead of with a connected account. Indirect charges include destination charges and separate charges and transfers) without setting `on_behalf_of`, interfaces use the platform’s branding settings unless explicitly overridden (such as when specifying a Checkout Session’s [branding_settings](https://docs.stripe.com/api/checkout/sessions/object#checkout_session_object-branding_settings))\n- For integrations that use indirect charges and set `on_behalf_of`, most interfaces use the connected account’s branding settings unless explicitly overridden. Connect-related emails sent to a connected account, such as risk or onboarding communications, are an exception. If you use the *customer portal* (The customer portal is a secure, Stripe-hosted page that lets your customers manage their subscriptions and billing details), you need to set [on_behalf_of](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customer_portal/sessions/create#create_portal_session-on_behalf_of) on the `CustomerPortalSession`. The customer portal only includes subscriptions and invoices whose `on_behalf_of` matches the value set on the session.\n> #### Self-branding\n>\n> Connect platforms and non-Connect users can’t configure their own branding using the Accounts API. They need to use the Dashboard.\n## Customize policies and contact information\nYou can display your return, refund, and legal policies, and your support contact information to your customers on Checkout. Go to [Checkout Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/checkout) to configure the information you want to display, including:\n- Details about your return and refund policies\n- Your support phone number, email, and website\n- Links to your terms of service and privacy policy\nPresenting this information can increase customer confidence and minimize cart abandonment.\n### Configure support and legal policies\nFrom [Checkout Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/checkout), add support contact information to your sessions by enabling **Contact information**. Similarly, add links to your **Terms of service** and **Privacy policy** to your sessions by enabling **Legal policies**. If you require customers to implicitly consent to your legal policies when they complete their checkout, select the **Display agreement to legal terms** checkbox.\nYou must add your support contact information and legal policy links in your [Public Detail Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/public).\nThe following previews show how Checkout displays a dialog with the support contact information, links to the store legal policies, and information about the payment terms.\n![A checkout page with contact information.](images/checkout/policies/contact-modal.png)\nPreview of contact information on Checkout.\n![A checkout page with legal policies.](images/checkout/policies/legal-modal.png)\nPreview of legal policies on Checkout.\n### Configure return and refund policies\nDisplay your return, refund, or exchange policies, by enabling **Return and Refund policies**. Although businesses that sell physical goods use return policies, businesses that sell digital goods or customized physical goods typically use refund policies. Because they’re not mutually exclusive, you can select both options if your business sells both categories of goods. You can edit your return and refund details, including:\n- Whether you accept returns, refunds, or exchanges\n- Whether returns, refunds, or exchanges are free or if they’re subject to a fee\n- How many days after a purchase you’ll accept returns, refunds, or exchanges\n- How customers can return items shipped to them\n- Whether you accept in-store returns\n- A link to the full return and refund policy\n- A custom message\nIf you accept free returns, refunds, or exchanges, Checkout highlights the policy for customers.\nThe following previews show how Checkout displays a return policy. In this example, it’s for purchases that can be returned by shipping them or in-store for a full refund (or exchange) for up to 60 days. You can display similar information for refunds.\n![Preview of return policies on Checkout](images/checkout/policies/return-policy-modal.png)\nPreview of return policies on Checkout.\n![Preview of a policy highlight on Checkout](images/checkout/policies/policy-highlight.png)\nPreview of a policy highlight on Checkout.\n## Other customization options\n- **Custom domains**\nCheckout, Payment Links, and customer portal pages use stripe.com as the default domain. You can optionally set up your own [custom domain](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout/custom-domains) for those products.\n- **Custom email domain**\nBy default, when Stripe sends invoices, receipts, and failed payment notifications to your customers, it sends them from the stripe.com domain. Set up your own [custom domain](https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/email-domain) to change this.\n- **Payments, debits, and bank transfer emails**\nYou can decide which emails your customers receive about payments, debits, and bank transfers in your [Customer emails settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/emails). You can also choose the default language to use for emails when you don’t know a customer’s preference.\n- **Billing (subscription and invoicing) emails**\nYou can turn on customer emails for [Billing](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/customer-emails) and [Invoicing](https://docs.stripe.com/invoicing/send-email) in the Dashboard or through the API."},{"title":"Build a payments page","subtitle":"Create a payments page with prebuilt UIs using the Checkout Sessions API.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout","type":"docs","content":"# Build a payments page\nCreate a payments page with prebuilt UIs using the Checkout Sessions API.\n## Accept payments on your website\nAccept one-time and subscription payments from more than 125 local payment methods.\n[Start building your checkout integration](https://docs.stripe.com/checkout/quickstart)\n## Stripe Checkout\nYou can use three payment UIs with the Checkout Sessions API. (api-integration: checkout)","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout","type":"docs","content":"Elements Appearance API: Checkout Sessions API\nCustomize the look and feel of Elements to match the design of your site. (api-integration: checkout)\nStripe Elements supports visual customization, which allows you to match the design of your site with the `appearance` option. The layout of each Element stays consistent, but you can modify colors, fonts, borders, padding, and more.\n1. Pick a prebuilt [theme](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#theme) that most closely resembles your website.\n1. Customize the theme using [inputs and labels](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#inputs-and-labels). You can also set [variables](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#variables), such as the `fontFamily` and `colorPrimary` to broadly customize components appearing throughout each Element.\n1. If needed, fine-tune individual components and states using [rules](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#rules).\nFor complete control, specify custom CSS properties for individual components appearing in the Element.\n> The Elements Appearance API doesn’t support individual payment method Elements (such as `CardElement`). Use the [Style](https://docs.stripe.com/js/appendix/style) object to customize your Element instead.\n## Themes\n- `stripe`\n- `night`\n- `flat`\n## Inputs and labels\nCustomize the appearance of input fields and their associated labels.\n`const appearance = {\ninputs: 'spaced',\nlabels: 'auto'\n}`\n### Inputs\nChoose the style of input fields to suit your design.\n| Variant     | Description                                                           |\n| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `spaced`    | Each input field has space surrounding it.                            |\n| `condensed` | Related input fields are grouped together without space between them. |\n### Labels\nControl the position and visibility of labels associated with input fields.\n| Variant    | Description                                                                                                                                                             |\n| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `auto`     | Labels adjust based on the input variant. When inputs are `spaced`, labels are `above`. When inputs are `condensed`, labels are `floating`. This is the default option. |\n| `above`    | Labels are positioned above the corresponding input fields.                                                                                                             |\n| `floating` | Labels float within the input fields.                                                                                                                                   |"},{"title":"Receipts and paid invoices","subtitle":"Send customer receipts for payments or refunds.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/receipts","type":"docs","content":"Customize receipts\nYou can customize your receipts to match your business’s visual design, along with the business information to display.\n### Branding\nYour branding settings control the visual display of your receipts and other Stripe interfaces.\n1. In the Dashboard, go to **Settings** > **Business** > [Branding](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/branding).\n1. Click the **Email receipts** tab.\n1. For the image type you want to add, click the plus icon (:plus:), then select your file. Make sure it meets all the [requirements](https://docs.stripe.com/receipts#image-requirements).\n1. For your color scheme, select your brand color and your accent color. You can use the dropdown color picker, or provide a color code as HEX or RGB values.\n1. Click **Save changes**.\n#### Image requirements\nImage requirements are the same for both the logo and icon files, but the icon is displayed at smaller sizes.\n| Dimensions           | - Must be square\n- Minimum 128 x 128 pixels |\n| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |\n| Supported file types | - PNG (recommended)\n- JPG                   |\n| Maximum file size    | 512 KB                                        |\n### Business information\nYour business details control the information that displays on receipts and other Stripe interfaces.\n1. In the Dashboard, go to **Settings** > **Business** > [Business details](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/business).\n1. Under **Public details**, click **Edit**.\n1. Update your customer support information, noting the [requirements](https://docs.stripe.com/receipts#support-requirements).\n1. Click **Save**.\n#### Support requirements\nFor compliance reasons, some contact information is always required on receipts:\n- Legal business name\n- Customer support address\n- Customer support email\n- Privacy policy URL\n### Localization\nThe language of the receipt and invoice is determined by the customer information available when you create the checkout session.\n| Customer information                                                       | Localization setting                                                                                                                        |\n| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Customer has [Account v2](https://docs.stripe.com/api/v2/core/accounts).   | Invoice uses value of [defaults.locales](https://docs.stripe.com/api/v2/core/accounts/object#v2_account_object-defaults-locales) attribute. |\n| Customer has [Customer account v1](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customers). | Invoice uses value of [preferred_locales](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customers/object#customer_object-preferred_locales) attribute.        |\n| Customer has no locale data available.                                     | Invoice uses **Default language** from your [**Customer emails** locale when they open the checkout session URL.                                                      |\n### Custom invoice data\nWhen creating a checkout session, you can pass custom values to the customer-facing elements.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/branding","type":"docs","content":"# Branding your Stripe account\nCustomize the appearance of your Stripe account and customer-facing elements.\nCustomize the appearance of your emails, checkout, payment links, customer portal, and invoices in your [Branding settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/account/branding).\n> #### Customize with an agent\n>\n> You can view and update your branding settings with the [Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli) or the [Stripe MCP server](https://docs.stripe.com/mcp). To find the available operations, run `stripe tools search branding` in the CLI, or ask your AI agent to search for `branding` using Stripe MCP.\n[Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IWpbEcdocUI)\n## Branding\nIcons and logos must be in JPG or PNG format, less than 512kb in size, and equal to or greater than 128px by 128px.\n- **Icon**—A square, digital-friendly icon or logo.\n- **Logo**—A non-square logo to override some uses of the icon.\n- **Brand color**—Used on receipts, invoices, and the customer portal.\n- **Accent color**—Used as a background on emails and pages.\n### Apply brand settings\nBrand settings apply to your whole account and take effect in many places.\n| Setting          | Emails                 | Checkout & Payment Links | Customer portal | Hosted invoice page | Invoice PDFs |\n| ---------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------- | ------------------- | ------------ |\n| **Icon**         | Yes                    | Yes                      | Yes             | Yes                 | Yes          |\n| **Logo**         | No                     | Yes                      | No              | No                  | Yes          |\n| **Brand color**  | Yes                    | No                       | Yes             | Yes                 | Yes          |\n| **Accent color** | Yes (background color) | Yes                      | Yes             | Yes                 | No           |\n### Branding with Connect\nConnect platforms can configure a connected account’s branding using [configuration.merchant.branding](https://docs.stripe.com/api/v2/core/accounts/object#v2_account_object-configuration-merchant-branding) (with the Accounts v2 API) or [settings.branding](https://docs.stripe.com/api/accounts/object#account_object-settings-branding) (with the Accounts v1 API). The branding of a given user interface depends on the integration:\n- For integrations that use *direct charges* (A charge type where customers transact directly with a connected account, which is always the merchant of record. With each payment, the connected account pays fees to Stripe and, optionally, to your platform), where objects usually exist on connected accounts, most interfaces use the connected account’s branding. Connect-related emails sent to a connected account, such as risk or onboarding communications, are an exception. Those emails use the platform’s branding.\n- For integrations that use *indirect charges* (A charge type where customers transact directly with your platform instead of with a connected account. Indirect charges include destination charges and separate charges and transfers) without setting `on_behalf_of`, interfaces use the platform’s branding settings unless explicitly overridden (such as when specifying a Checkout Session’s [branding_settings](https://docs.stripe.com/api/checkout/sessions/object#checkout_session_object-branding_settings))\n- For integrations that use indirect charges and set `on_behalf_of`, most interfaces use the connected account’s branding settings unless explicitly overridden. Connect-related emails sent to a connected account, such as risk or onboarding communications, are an exception. If you use the *customer portal* (The customer portal is a secure, Stripe-hosted page that lets your customers manage their subscriptions and billing details), you need to set [on_behalf_of](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customer_portal/sessions/create#create_portal_session-on_behalf_of) on the `CustomerPortalSession`. The customer portal only includes subscriptions and invoices whose `on_behalf_of` matches the value set on the session.\n> #### Self-branding\n>\n> Connect platforms and non-Connect users can’t configure their own branding using the Accounts API. They need to use the Dashboard.\n## Customize policies and contact information\nYou can display your return, refund, and legal policies, and your support contact information to your customers on Checkout. Go to [Checkout Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/checkout) to configure the information you want to display, including:\n- Details about your return and refund policies\n- Your support phone number, email, and website\n- Links to your terms of service and privacy policy\nPresenting this information can increase customer confidence and minimize cart abandonment.\n### Configure support and legal policies\nFrom [Checkout Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/checkout), add support contact information to your sessions by enabling **Contact information**. Similarly, add links to your **Terms of service** and **Privacy policy** to your sessions by enabling **Legal policies**. If you require customers to implicitly consent to your legal policies when they complete their checkout, select the **Display agreement to legal terms** checkbox.\nYou must add your support contact information and legal policy links in your [Public Detail Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/public).\nThe following previews show how Checkout displays a dialog with the support contact information, links to the store legal policies, and information about the payment terms.\n![A checkout page with contact information.](images/checkout/policies/contact-modal.png)\nPreview of contact information on Checkout.\n![A checkout page with legal policies.](images/checkout/policies/legal-modal.png)\nPreview of legal policies on Checkout.\n### Configure return and refund policies\nDisplay your return, refund, or exchange policies, by enabling **Return and Refund policies**. Although businesses that sell physical goods use return policies, businesses that sell digital goods or customized physical goods typically use refund policies. Because they’re not mutually exclusive, you can select both options if your business sells both categories of goods. You can edit your return and refund details, including:\n- Whether you accept returns, refunds, or exchanges\n- Whether returns, refunds, or exchanges are free or if they’re subject to a fee\n- How many days after a purchase you’ll accept returns, refunds, or exchanges\n- How customers can return items shipped to them\n- Whether you accept in-store returns\n- A link to the full return and refund policy\n- A custom message\nIf you accept free returns, refunds, or exchanges, Checkout highlights the policy for customers.\nThe following previews show how Checkout displays a return policy. In this example, it’s for purchases that can be returned by shipping them or in-store for a full refund (or exchange) for up to 60 days. You can display similar information for refunds.\n![Preview of return policies on Checkout](images/checkout/policies/return-policy-modal.png)\nPreview of return policies on Checkout.\n![Preview of a policy highlight on Checkout](images/checkout/policies/policy-highlight.png)\nPreview of a policy highlight on Checkout.\n## Other customization options\n- **Custom domains**\nCheckout, Payment Links, and customer portal pages use stripe.com as the default domain. You can optionally set up your own [custom domain](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout/custom-domains) for those products.\n- **Custom email domain**\nBy default, when Stripe sends invoices, receipts, and failed payment notifications to your customers, it sends them from the stripe.com domain. Set up your own [custom domain](https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/email-domain) to change this.\n- **Payments, debits, and bank transfer emails**\nYou can decide which emails your customers receive about payments, debits, and bank transfers in your [Customer emails settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/emails). You can also choose the default language to use for emails when you don’t know a customer’s preference.\n- **Billing (subscription and invoicing) emails**\nYou can turn on customer emails for [Billing](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/customer-emails) and [Invoicing](https://docs.stripe.com/invoicing/send-email) in the Dashboard or through the API."},{"title":"Build a payments page","subtitle":"Create a payments page with prebuilt UIs using the Checkout Sessions API.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout","type":"docs","content":"# Build a payments page\nCreate a payments page with prebuilt UIs using the Checkout Sessions API.\n## Accept payments on your website\nAccept one-time and subscription payments from more than 125 local payment methods.\n[Start building your checkout integration](https://docs.stripe.com/checkout/quickstart)\n## Stripe Checkout\nYou can use three payment UIs with the Checkout Sessions API. Customize the theme using [inputs and labels](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#inputs-and-labels). You can also set [variables](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#variables), such as the `fontFamily` and `colorPrimary` to broadly customize components appearing throughout each Element.\n1. If needed, fine-tune individual components and states using [rules](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#rules).\nFor complete control, specify custom CSS properties for individual components appearing in the Element.\n> The Elements Appearance API doesn’t support individual payment method Elements (such as `CardElement`). Use the [Style](https://docs.stripe.com/js/appendix/style) object to customize your Element instead.\n## Themes\n- `stripe`\n- `night`\n- `flat`\n## Inputs and labels\nCustomize the appearance of input fields and their associated labels.\n`const appearance = {\ninputs: 'spaced',\nlabels: 'auto'\n}`\n### Inputs\nChoose the style of input fields to suit your design.\n| Variant     | Description                                                           |\n| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `spaced`    | Each input field has space surrounding it.                            |\n| `condensed` | Related input fields are grouped together without space between them. |\n### Labels\nControl the position and visibility of labels associated with input fields.\n| Variant    | Description                                                                                                                                                             |\n| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `auto`     | Labels adjust based on the input variant. This is the default option. |\n| `above`    | Labels are positioned above the corresponding input fields.                                                                                                             |\n| `floating` | Labels float within the input fields.                                                                                                                                   |"},{"title":"Receipts and paid invoices","subtitle":"Send customer receipts for payments or refunds.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/receipts","type":"docs","content":"Customize receipts\nYou can customize your receipts to match your business’s visual design, along with the business information to display.\n### Branding\nYour branding settings control the visual display of your receipts and other Stripe interfaces.\n1. In the Dashboard, go to **Settings** > **Business** > [Branding](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/branding).\n1. Click the **Email receipts** tab.\n1. For the image type you want to add, click the plus icon (:plus:), then select your file. Make sure it meets all the [requirements](https://docs.stripe.com/receipts#image-requirements).\n1. For your color scheme, select your brand color and your accent color. You can use the dropdown color picker, or provide a color code as HEX or RGB values.\n1. Click **Save changes**.\n#### Image requirements\nImage requirements are the same for both the logo and icon files, but the icon is displayed at smaller sizes.\n| Dimensions           | - Must be square\n- Minimum 128 x 128 pixels |\n| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |\n| Supported file types | - PNG (recommended)\n- JPG                   |\n| Maximum file size    | 512 KB                                        |\n### Business information\nYour business details control the information that displays on receipts and other Stripe interfaces.\n1. In the Dashboard, go to **Settings** > **Business** > [Business details](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/business).\n1. Under **Public details**, click **Edit**.\n1. Update your customer support information, noting the [requirements](https://docs.stripe.com/receipts#support-requirements).\n1. Click **Save**.\n#### Support requirements\nFor compliance reasons, some contact information is always required on receipts:\n- Legal business name\n- Customer support address\n- Customer support email\n- Privacy policy URL\n### Localization\nThe language of the receipt and invoice is determined by the customer information available when you create the checkout session.\n| Customer information ## What’s new
Adds the [branding_settings](https://docs.stripe.com/api/checkout/sessions/object?api-version=2025-09-30.clover#checkout_session_object-branding_settings) parameter to [Checkout Sessions](https://docs.stripe.com/api/checkout/sessions?api-version=2025-09-30.clover).

You can now apply custom branding to a Checkout Session by using the [branding_settings](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout/customization/appearance?payment-ui=stripe-hosted&integration=api#branding) parameter to:
- Set a logo or icon
- Customize the Checkout page’s background color, button color, font, and shapes
- Change your brand name
You can use this parameter to override the business’s branding settings for a Checkout Session.

Customize the appearance of your Stripe account and customer-facing elements.
Customize the appearance of your emails, checkout, payment links, customer portal, and invoices in your [Branding settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/account/branding).
> #### Customize with an agent
>
> You can view and update your branding settings with the [Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli) or the [Stripe MCP server](https://docs.stripe.com/mcp). To find the available operations, run `stripe tools search branding` in the CLI, or ask your AI agent to search for `branding` using Stripe MCP.
[Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IWpbEcdocUI)
## Branding
Icons and logos must be in JPG or PNG format, less than 512kb in size, and equal to or greater than 128px by 128px.
- **Icon**—A square, digital-friendly icon or logo.
- **Logo**—A non-square logo to override some uses of the icon.
- **Brand color**—Used on receipts, invoices, and the customer portal.
- **Accent color**—Used as a background on emails and pages.
### Apply brand settings
Brand settings apply to your whole account and take effect in many places.
| Setting          | Emails                 | Checkout & Payment Links | Customer portal | Hosted invoice page | Invoice PDFs |
| ---------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------- | ------------------- | ------------ |
| **Icon**         | Yes                    | Yes                      | Yes             | Yes                 | Yes          |
| **Logo**         | No                     | Yes                      | No              | No                  | Yes          |
| **Brand color**  | Yes                    | No                       | Yes             | Yes                 | Yes          |
| **Accent color** | Yes (background color) | Yes                      | Yes             | Yes                 | No           |
### Branding with Connect
Connect platforms can configure a connected account’s branding using [configuration.merchant.branding](https://docs.stripe.com/api/v2/core/accounts/object#v2_account_object-configuration-merchant-branding) (with the Accounts v2 API) or [settings.branding](https://docs.stripe.com/api/accounts/object#account_object-settings-branding) (with the Accounts v1 API). The branding of a given user interface depends on the integration:
- For integrations that use *direct charges* (A charge type where customers transact directly with a connected account, which is always the merchant of record. With each payment, the connected account pays fees to Stripe and, optionally, to your platform), where objects usually exist on connected accounts, most interfaces use the connected account’s branding. Connect-related emails sent to a connected account, such as risk or onboarding communications, are an exception. Those emails use the platform’s branding.
- For integrations that use *indirect charges* (A charge type where customers transact directly with your platform instead of with a connected account. Indirect charges include destination charges and separate charges and transfers) without setting `on_behalf_of`, interfaces use the platform’s branding settings unless explicitly overridden (such as when specifying a Checkout Session’s [branding_settings](https://docs.stripe.com/api/checkout/sessions/object#checkout_session_object-branding_settings))
- For integrations that use indirect charges and set `on_behalf_of`, most interfaces use the connected account’s branding settings unless explicitly overridden. Connect-related emails sent to a connected account, such as risk or onboarding communications, are an exception. If you use the *customer portal* (The customer portal is a secure, Stripe-hosted page that lets your customers manage their subscriptions and billing details), you need to set [on_behalf_of](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customer_portal/sessions/create#create_portal_session-on_behalf_of) on the `CustomerPortalSession`. The customer portal only includes subscriptions and invoices whose `on_behalf_of` matches the value set on the session.
> #### Self-branding
>
> Connect platforms and non-Connect users can’t configure their own branding using the Accounts API. They need to use the Dashboard.
## Customize policies and contact information
You can display your return, refund, and legal policies, and your support contact information to your customers on Checkout. Go to [Checkout Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/checkout) to configure the information you want to display, including:
- Details about your return and refund policies
- Your support phone number, email, and website
- Links to your terms of service and privacy policy
Presenting this information can increase customer confidence and minimize cart abandonment.
### Configure support and legal policies
From [Checkout Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/checkout), add support contact information to your sessions by enabling **Contact information**. Similarly, add links to your **Terms of service** and **Privacy policy** to your sessions by enabling **Legal policies**. If you require customers to implicitly consent to your legal policies when they complete their checkout, select the **Display agreement to legal terms** checkbox.
You must add your support contact information and legal policy links in your [Public Detail Settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/public).
The following previews show how Checkout displays a dialog with the support contact information, links to the store legal policies, and information about the payment terms.
![A checkout page with contact information.](images/checkout/policies/contact-modal.png)
Preview of contact information on Checkout.
![A checkout page with legal policies.](images/checkout/policies/legal-modal.png)
Preview of legal policies on Checkout.
### Configure return and refund policies
Display your return, refund, or exchange policies, by enabling **Return and Refund policies**. Although businesses that sell physical goods use return policies, businesses that sell digital goods or customized physical goods typically use refund policies. Because they’re not mutually exclusive, you can select both options if your business sells both categories of goods. You can edit your return and refund details, including:
- Whether you accept returns, refunds, or exchanges
- Whether returns, refunds, or exchanges are free or if they’re subject to a fee
- How many days after a purchase you’ll accept returns, refunds, or exchanges
- How customers can return items shipped to them
- Whether you accept in-store returns
- A link to the full return and refund policy
- A custom message
If you accept free returns, refunds, or exchanges, Checkout highlights the policy for customers.
The following previews show how Checkout displays a return policy. In this example, it’s for purchases that can be returned by shipping them or in-store for a full refund (or exchange) for up to 60 days. You can display similar information for refunds.
![Preview of return policies on Checkout](images/checkout/policies/return-policy-modal.png)
Preview of return policies on Checkout.
![Preview of a policy highlight on Checkout](images/checkout/policies/policy-highlight.png)
Preview of a policy highlight on Checkout.
## Other customization options
- **Custom domains**
Checkout, Payment Links, and customer portal pages use stripe.com as the default domain. You can optionally set up your own [custom domain](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout/custom-domains) for those products.
- **Custom email domain**
By default, when Stripe sends invoices, receipts, and failed payment notifications to your customers, it sends them from the stripe.com domain. Set up your own [custom domain](https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/email-domain) to change this.
- **Payments, debits, and bank transfer emails**
You can decide which emails your customers receive about payments, debits, and bank transfers in your [Customer emails settings](https://dashboard.stripe.com/settings/emails). You can also choose the default language to use for emails when you don’t know a customer’s preference.
- **Billing (subscription and invoicing) emails**
You can turn on customer emails for [Billing](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/customer-emails) and [Invoicing](https://docs.stripe.com/invoicing/send-email) in the Dashboard or through the API."},{"title":"Build a payments page","subtitle":"Create a payments page with prebuilt UIs using the Checkout Sessions API.","url":"https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout","type":"docs","content":"# Build a payments page

Stripe Elements supports visual customization, which allows you to match the design of your site with the `appearance` option. The layout of each Element stays consistent, but you can modify colors, fonts, borders, padding, and more.
1. Pick a prebuilt [theme](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#theme) that most closely resembles your website.
1. Customize the theme using [inputs and labels](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#inputs-and-labels). You can also set [variables](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#variables), such as the `fontFamily` and `colorPrimary` to broadly customize components appearing throughout each Element.
1. If needed, fine-tune individual components and states using [rules](https://docs.stripe.com/elements/appearance-api?api-integration=checkout#rules).
For complete control, specify custom CSS properties for individual components appearing in the Element.
> The Elements Appearance API doesn’t support individual payment method Elements (such as `CardElement`). Use the [Style](https://docs.stripe.com/js/appendix/style) object to customize your Element instead.

Customize the appearance of input fields and their associated labels.

labels: 'auto'
}`
### Inputs
Choose the style of input fields to suit your design.
| Variant     | Description                                                           |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `spaced`    | Each input field has space surrounding it.                            |
| `condensed` | Related input fields are grouped together without space between them. |
### Labels

| `above`    | Labels are positioned above the corresponding input fields.                                                                                                             |
